metadata.title: Updated IQ and Well-Being Scores for the 50 U.S. States

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not analyze individual-level PIAAC or NAEP microdata with a complex survey design; instead, it uses published state-level literacy/numeracy and reading/math results to construct aggregate state IQ and then correlates these aggregates with other state indicators. Because the unit of analysis is the 50 U.S. states (ecological/state-level data), standard student sampling weights (e.g., PIAAC/NAEP design weights) are not applied in the reported analyses. The paper also does not report any replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife) or any explicit weighting variable name. Consequently, the results should be interpreted as descriptive/correlational evidence at the state level rather than as population-representative estimates derived from weighted student-level modeling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are generated for cognitive achievement scales in ILSA microdata, but this paper constructs state-level IQ and well-being indices from already-aggregated state scores and then reports correlations among state-level composites. Since the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement outcomes at the student level, PV handling is not applicable to the reported analyses. The paper also does not describe any missing-data imputation or deletion rules because it does not perform student-level model estimation with missingness in the analysis dataset; it relies on compiled state-level indicators from external sources.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Unit of analysis is the 50 U.S. states. State IQ is derived by averaging two state-level IQ components: (a) PIAAC Literacy and Numeracy-based state IQ using PIAAC results for 2012–2017, and (b) NAEP Math and Reading-based state IQ using NAEP results for 2015, 2017, and 2019 (fourth and eighth grade). State well-being is constructed from four well-being subdomains (crime, education, health, income) using principal components analyses on multiple state-level indicators per subdomain, followed by a hierarchical PCA to obtain a global well-being component. The paper does not report any additional inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond using the specified years/sources for the state-level indicators.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict well-being, finding that This paper updates previously published state-level IQ and well-being estimates for the 50 U.S. states by combining aggregate results from two large-scale assessments: PIAAC (adult Literacy and Numeracy; 2012–2017) and NAEP (fourth/eighth grade Math and Reading; 2015, 2017, 2019). It constructs state IQ by averaging PIAAC- and NAEP-derived state IQ components, then builds well-being from four subdomains (crime, education, health, income) using principal components analyses and a hierarchical PCA to obtain a global well-being index. The reported results are correlations and variance-explained statistics (e.g., global well-being explaining 75% of variance across subdomains; state IQ correlating 0.80 with global well-being; state IQ correlating up to 0.87 with FICO credit scores). No machine learning model is trained; therefore, there are no predictive performance metrics, no PV handling for student-level outcomes, and no survey-weighted estimation. The main limitation is ecological inference risk: state-level correlations may not translate to individual-level causal effects. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The study is an ecological/state-level data construction and correlational analysis rather than an empirical ML prediction paper. As a result, there is no student-level analytic sample size, no ML algorithm training/evaluation, and no PV-based outcome modeling. The paper also does not report missing-data handling because it does not perform student-level estimation with missingness; it compiles external state indicators and then applies PCA-based scale construction and correlation analyses.
